_about: Decision table for SN1/SN2/E1/E2. Rows are checked in order and the first match wins. when: lg (halide | sulfonate | OH), cls (methyl | 1 | 2 | 3), ab (allylic/benzylic), box (nuc | nucbase | bulky | weak | activator), act (HX | PBr3 | SOCl2 | TsCl | MsCl | acid), solvent (protic | aprotic), heat (true | false). A missing key matches anything; a list matches any of its values. lamps: major | minor | competing (missing = doesn't happen). notCovered: a reason key instead of a prediction. activate: the step only turns OH into a leaving group.

reasons.methyl_sn2: A methyl carbon is completely open to backside attack and has no β-hydrogens, so SN2 is the only path.
reasons.methyl_weak: A weak nucleophile is too slow for SN2, and a methyl cation is far too unstable for SN1, so no useful reaction happens.
reasons.primary_sn2: A 1° carbon is easy to reach from the back, and this nucleophile is a weak base, so SN2 wins.
reasons.strong_base_some_e2: The reagent is also a strong base, so a little E2 competes, but on an unhindered 1° carbon substitution still wins.
reasons.bulky_base: A bulky base is too crowded to reach the carbon from the back, so it pulls off a β-hydrogen instead (E2), taking the most reachable one (Hofmann).
reasons.ab_cation: Next to a C=C or benzene ring the carbocation is stabilised by resonance, so even this 1° carbon can ionise.
reasons.primary_weak: A weak nucleophile is too slow for SN2, and a 1° carbocation is too unstable for SN1, so no useful reaction happens.
reasons.secondary_good_nuc: A good nucleophile that is a weak base attacks the 2° carbon from the back (SN2) instead of removing a proton.
reasons.course_ab_aprotic_sn2: Course rule (worksheet 3c): a 2° allylic/benzylic halide with an alkoxide in a polar aprotic solvent gives SN2 as the major path; E2 competes.
reasons.secondary_strong_base: A strong base meeting a crowded 2° carbon removes a β-hydrogen more easily than it attacks the carbon, so E2 is major.
reasons.books_disagree_2: Textbooks differ on 2° substrates with strong, unhindered bases; most give E2 major and SN2 minor.
reasons.hofmann_2_varies: With 2° substrates, textbooks vary on how strongly the bulky base favours the less substituted alkene.
reasons.course_weak_protic_heat: Course rule (worksheet 3d): a weak nucleophile in a polar protic solvent gives SN1 as the major answer even with heat; E1 competes. The protic solvent holds the nucleophile back, so the leaving group leaves on its own first.
reasons.weak_protic_sn1: The weak nucleophile can't push the leaving group out, so the leaving group leaves first (carbocation), helped by the polar protic solvent, and the solvent then attacks (SN1).
reasons.weak_aprotic: A weak nucleophile without a polar protic solvent to stabilise a carbocation isn't covered yet.
reasons.tertiary_no_sn2: A 3° carbon is too crowded for backside attack, so SN2 can't happen.
reasons.tertiary_strong_base: A strong base removes a β-hydrogen from the crowded 3° substrate: E2.
reasons.course_3_ab_aprotic_sn1: Your course (Ch 6 test, 2a): a 3° benzylic or allylic carbon is too crowded for SN2, but its cation is so stable that SN1 happens even in a polar aprotic solvent like DMSO. The product is racemic. The same cation can also lose a β-H (E1); that is shown as minor because the good nucleophile traps the cation first. A plain 3° halide with a good nucleophile in an aprotic solvent is still not covered: textbooks disagree.
reasons.tertiary_nuc_aprotic: A 3° substrate with a good nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent isn't covered yet: textbooks don't agree on one answer.
reasons.oh_protonated: OH⁻ is a poor leaving group, so the acid first protonates the OH; water (H₂O) is a good leaving group.
reasons.hx_primary: On a 1° alcohol, the halide then attacks from the back (SN2): a 1° carbocation is too unstable.
reasons.hx_secondary_tertiary: On a 2° or 3° alcohol, water leaves first to give a carbocation (which can shift), and the halide adds to it (SN1).
reasons.hx_why_not_sn2: Why can't the halide push water out from the back at the same moment (SN2)? Both paths start from the same OH₂⁺; it is a race. SN2 needs the halide to hit the back of the carbon exactly as water leaves. SN1 lets water leave on its own first. On a 2° or 3° carbon, water wins: it is a very good leaving group (neutral), the cation is stable enough to form (carbons on C⁺ feed it electrons), the carbon groups crowd the back, and in the acidic water the halide is held back by hydrogen bonds.
reasons.hx_evidence: Evidence for the carbocation: when a hydride or methyl shift can make a more stable cation, the halide ends up on the neighbouring carbon (3-methylbutan-2-ol + HBr → 2-bromo-2-methylbutane). SN2 only swaps groups on one carbon, so a shifted product proves a cation formed. Compare butan-1-ol + HBr: a 1° cation is too unstable, so there it is SN2 (one hump, two arrows at once). For 2° alcohols this is the textbook rule; real reactions can also give a little SN2.
reasons.hx_no_e1: The halide is a good nucleophile and a very weak base, so substitution wins over elimination.
reasons.pbr3_socl2: PBr₃ / SOCl₂ turn the OH into a good leaving group on oxygen, then the halide attacks from the back (SN2, inversion). No carbocation, so no shifts.
reasons.pbr3_tertiary: PBr₃ and SOCl₂ work by SN2, which a 3° alcohol can't do; this case isn't covered.
reasons.sulfonate_ester: TsCl/MsCl with pyridine turn the OH into a sulfonate ester (OTs/OMs), an excellent leaving group. Only the O–H bond reacts, so the carbon keeps its configuration (retention).
reasons.acid_dehydration: With a non-nucleophilic acid and heat, water leaves to give a carbocation and a β-hydrogen is lost (E1, Zaitsev). The conjugate base (HSO₄⁻ / H₂PO₄⁻) is too weak a nucleophile to substitute.
reasons.acid_primary: Acid dehydration of a 1° alcohol goes by a different (E2-like) path at high temperature; not covered yet.
reasons.acid_no_heat: Without heat, H₂SO₄/H₃PO₄ with an alcohol doesn't give a clean elimination; not covered yet.
reasons.oh_poor_lg: OH⁻ is a poor leaving group, so nothing happens until the OH is activated (HX, PBr₃, SOCl₂, TsCl, or acid + heat).
reasons.activator_not_alcohol: This reagent is used to activate alcohols; using it on this substrate isn't covered.
reasons.vinyl_aryl: The leaving group is on an sp² carbon (vinyl or aryl): backside attack is blocked and the cation would be very unstable, so no SN1, SN2, E1 or E2.
reasons.neopentyl: Neopentyl-type 1° carbon: the bulky group next door blocks backside attack, so SN2 is extremely slow, and SN1 would need a 1° carbocation (which would rearrange). Not covered.
reasons.poor_lg: Fluoride is a very poor leaving group; this isn't covered.
reasons.alpha_group: A C=O or heteroatom on the reacting carbon changes the rules; not covered yet.
reasons.no_site: No leaving group was found (Cl, Br, I, OTs, OMs, or an alcohol OH on an sp³ carbon).
reasons.no_beta_h: There is no β-hydrogen to remove, so elimination can't happen.
reasons.no_nu: This reagent has no nucleophilic atom that can bond to carbon here.
reasons.ring_e2_warning: May differ: the trans-diaxial requirement isn't checked yet; see the Chair tab.
reasons.e2_beta_stereo: Here the anti-periplanar geometry decides E vs Z (the β-carbon is a defined stereocentre); not covered yet.
reasons.allylic_e1: E1 from an allylic cation (dienes) isn't covered yet.
reasons.promoted: The pathway above can't happen here, so the next one becomes the major path.
reasons.ez_tie: The E and Z alkenes can't be told apart by bulk here, so neither is favoured: shown as competing.
reasons.ring_contraction_not_covered: This shift would shrink the ring. Ring contraction isn't covered yet.
reasons.unknown_reagent: The reagent isn't in the list. Draw it so the rules can estimate its role.
reasons.unknown_solvent: Pick a solvent, so the rules know whether it is polar protic or polar aprotic.
reasons.no_rule: No row of the decision table covers this combination yet, so the app doesn't guess.
